title: Discipline and Habits
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/0/body: Pros repeat the same set of tasks every day so that **decisions are made in advance** and **habit** replaces excitement. A routine means fewer in-the-moment decisions and fewer mistakes.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/1/title: The three parts of a routine
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/1/body: **Before the market:** check the economic calendar, key levels and how you're feeling. **During the market:** only the setups in your plan. **After the market:** log your trades and review.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/2/prompt: Put a trading day's routine in order:
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/2/items/0: Prep: economic calendar and key levels
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/2/items/1: Wait for a setup that's in your plan
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/2/items/2: Enter with a set stop loss
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/2/items/3: Manage the open trade by the plan
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/2/items/4: Log the trade in your journal
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/2/explana: First you prepare, then you wait only for a setup from your plan, enter with a stop loss, manage the trade, and log everything at the end of the day.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/3/prompt: After a sleepless night and getting angry about something personal, you sit down at the charts. What does a good routine say to do?
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/3/options: Don't trade today, or trade much smaller
Keep going with your usual size
Trade bigger to cheer yourself up
Jump in fast without checking the calendar
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/3/explana: Checking your state of mind is part of preparing. Tiredness and anger cloud your judgment; on days you're not feeling right, trade less or not at all.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/4/title: Trading hours and a trade limit
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/4/body: Set yourself **fixed trading hours** and a **maximum number of trades per day**. When your hours are up or you hit the limit, close the platform, even if you see "a great opportunity."
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/4/tip: Write your pre-trade checklist and stick it next to your monitor.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/5/stateme: Checking the economic calendar before your day starts helps you avoid getting caught off guard by big news.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/5/explana: Big news can suddenly spike volatility. If you know the release times in advance, you can stay out or lower your risk.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/6/stateme: The more time you spend at the charts trading, the better your results will surely be.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/6/explana: Long hours mean fatigue and low-quality trades. Results come from the quality of your setups, not the number of trades.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/7/sentenc: A good routine has three parts: preparing ___ the market, executing your plan, and a ___ after the market.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/7/explana: Preparation stops emotional decisions, and reviewing helps you get a little better every day.
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/8/prompt: Which of these is NOT part of pre-market prep?
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/8/options: A warm-up trade to get into the groove
Checking your own state of mind
lessons/psychology-u3-l1/steps/8/explana: A "warm-up trade" means entering without a setup. Preparing means understanding the conditions, not trading.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/0/body: For every trade: **symbol, direction, entry, stop loss, take profit, size and result**, and most importantly your **reason for entering** and your **state of mind**. A screenshot of the chart at the moment you entered helps a lot too.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/1/title: R: the common language of results
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/1/body: Record your result in **R**: how many times your risk you won or lost. If you risked $20 and made $60, the result is **+3R**. That way, trades of different sizes become **comparable**.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/2/prompt: A trade risked $50 and closed with $100 profit. What's the result in R?
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/2/explana: 100 ÷ 50 = 2, so you made twice your risk: +2R.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/3/pairs/0: The setup that made you enter
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/3/pairs/2: Your result measured in units of risk
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/3/pairs/3: An image of the chart when you entered
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/4/body: A journal nobody reads is useless. At the end of each week, go over your trades, tag your **repeat mistakes** (like "entered too early") and pick just **one thing** to fix next week.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/4/tip: Judge yourself on "executing correctly," not just on profit and loss.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/5/stateme: Only losing trades are worth recording in your journal.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/5/explana: Winning trades need recording too: both to find the setups that really work, and because some wins came from breaking your rules.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/6/prompt: In your monthly review, you notice 7 of your 10 biggest losses were trades you opened after 11 p.m. What's the best conclusion?
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/6/options: Make a rule: no trading after 11 p.m.
Use more leverage on late-night trades
Stop journaling because it upsets you
Ignore it; it must be random
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/6/explana: That's exactly what a journal is for: finding a repeating pattern and turning it into a clear rule. Late-night fatigue is probably hurting the quality of your decisions.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/7/sentenc: In your journal, besides the trade's numbers, write down your ___ for entering and your ___ of mind.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/7/explana: The numbers tell you what happened; your reason for entering and your state of mind tell you why. Repeat mistakes usually show up in those two columns.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/8/stateme: Recording results in R helps you fairly compare trades of different sizes.
lessons/psychology-u3-l2/steps/8/explana: $100 profit on $100 of risk (+1R) is very different from $100 profit on $25 of risk (+4R). R shows that difference.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/0/title: Every trade is just one sample
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/0/body: Even the best setup isn't **guaranteed**. Your system makes money over **a long series of trades**, not on each one. Think like a casino owner: they might lose a hand, but over thousands of hands the **statistical edge** is on their side.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/1/body: A trade made **by the plan** that lost is a good trade. A trade made **without a plan** that won is a bad trade, because it reinforces a bad habit. Judge yourself by the **quality of your execution**.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/1/example: Fine; a cost of doing business
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/2/prompt: Your system has about a 50% win rate and a 1:2 risk-reward, and you've taken 4 losses in a row. What does a probabilistic mindset say?
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/2/options: Losing streaks are normal in any system; stick to the plan
The system is broken; switch it right now
Double your size to win it back faster
The next trade is sure to win; it's due
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/2/explana: With a 50% win rate, the chance of 4 losses in any specific run of 4 trades is about 6%, and over 100 trades it's very likely to happen somewhere. You judge a system on a big sample, not on 4 trades.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/3/stateme: After 5 losses in a row, the next trade is more likely to win because a win is "due."
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/3/explana: The market doesn't know about your past losses. The odds of your next trade depend on the quality of the setup, not on previous results. This false belief is called the gambler's fallacy.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/4/body: Most trading stress comes from **trading too big**. If a trade is keeping you up at night or you keep checking it, the risk is too much for your mind. **Trade smaller**, set **price alerts** instead of staring at the chart, and **take breaks** between trades.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/4/tip: If the thought of losing on this trade rattles you, your size is too big.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/5/sentenc: If a trade's outcome stresses you out a lot, its ___ is usually too big for your mind and should be ___.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/5/explana: When the amount at stake feels bearable, it's easier to decide by the plan, and your stress drops.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/6/stateme: A trade made exactly by the plan that closed at a loss isn't necessarily a bad trade.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/6/explana: Losses are part of every profitable system. If the setup, size and stop loss followed your plan, you did your job right.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/7/prompt: This trade, made exactly by the plan, first hit the stop loss (highlighted candle), and then the price went on to the take profit. What's the best reaction?
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/7/options: Log it and accept it as part of the odds
Trade without a stop loss from now on
Open a bigger trade right away to win it back
Drop the plan because it didn't work this time
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/7/explana: It hurts, but it's normal. Dropping your stop loss or revenge trading because of one result is exactly thinking based on a single sample. If your journal shows it happening again and again, that's when you review where you place your stop.
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/8/pairs/0: Thinking in terms of a series of trades
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/8/pairs/2: How well you execute your plan
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/9/prompt: You're hit by intense stress in the middle of a trade. Do these things in order:
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/9/items/0: Step away from the chart for a few minutes and breathe
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/9/items/1: Check your stop loss and take profit are in place
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/9/items/2: Ask: has the plan's invalidation point been hit?
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/9/items/3: Decide based on the plan's answer, not your feelings
lessons/psychology-u3-l3/steps/9/explana: First calm your mind, then make sure your risk is under control, then check the situation against your invalidation point, and decide based only on the plan.
